title: Rabbi Nachman's narrow bridge
hookLine: Hasidic, Sephardi and modern teachers kept the conversation going
carry: a narrow bridge, and not to be afraid
tomorrow: what if you feel the pull, and never once act on it?

cards: Graduation season. Caps on the counter, a group photo being planned, and someone at the edge of it wondering what happens once everyone scatters. Does the friendship end when the school does?
The same question can be asked of a tradition. When the Talmud was finished, did the conversation stop? It didn't.

teach.b: It works like one long table where new chairs keep getting pulled up.
Sephardi teachers, the Jews of Spain and their heirs, wrote law and philosophy; Maimonides wrote a full code of Jewish law and a book he called a guide for the perplexed.

Hasidic teachers in Eastern Europe taught through stories, melody and joy. One of them, Rabbi Nachman of Breslov, taught that a person must cross a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid.
Modern teachers kept going in new languages; Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a palace built in time.
One to tell a friend tonight: the version people sing says the whole world is a very narrow bridge, but his own text puts a person on the bridge. Here's what holds these later voices together.
Each one quotes the voices before. Maimonides cites the Talmud; the Hasidic masters cite the midrash you just spent forty days on. Nobody starts from scratch, and nobody just repeats.

teach.h: A NARROW BRIDGE, AND NOT TO BE AFRAID.
teach.b: For the next forty days, this block listens to them, beginning with a small book called the Tanya. The conversation didn't end when a book closed. It found new people to carry it, which is how it reached you.

how: Jewish study today mixes eras on one shelf: Torah and Talmud beside Maimonides, Hasidic teachings and modern writers, and many communities keep the customs of their Sephardi, Ashkenazi or Mizrahi ancestors.

practice: Read one line slowly, out loud, a few words at a time: a person must cross a very narrow bridge, and the main thing is not to be afraid. Say it once at your normal speed, then once with a breath between every few words.
Let the slow one be the version you keep.
